RID 5-STEP PROTOCOL 

STEP 1 — PRE-COMMITMENT  
Causal identification strategy: sharp regression-discontinuity design exploiting the discrete jump in treatment intensity at the 1 500-gram very-low-birth-weight (VLBW) threshold. Units just below 1 500 g receive substantially more neonatal care than units just above; in a sufficiently narrow bandwidth, birth-weight is as-good-as-random.

Directional hypothesis (H1): Crossing the VLBW threshold (BirthWeight < 1 500 g) – which increases medical treatment – lowers mortality. Formally, τ ≡ E[Mortality|BW = 1 500⁻] – E[Mortality|BW = 1 500⁺] < 0.

I will not change this strategy or hypothesis after this point.

STEP 2 — SPECIFICATION DISCIPLINE  
Exactly five and only five estimations will be run. All use a local linear RD with a triangular kernel and the Imbens–Kalyanaraman (IK) optimal bandwidth (computed separately for each outcome). The running variable is birth-weight in grams, centered at 1 500 g. All regressions include the following covariates interacted with the treatment indicator (covariate‐adjusted RD): gestational-age dummies (in weeks), infant sex, plurality indicator, maternal age (5-year bins), maternal race dummies, and birth year fixed effects.

Spec 1  First-stage: outcome = NICU_transfer (1 = ever transferred/admitted to higher-level NICU).  
Spec 2  Reduced form: outcome = 1-year mortality (death within 365 days).  
Spec 3  Reduced form: outcome = 28-day neonatal mortality.  
Spec 4  First-stage (resource use): outcome = log(hospital_charges) for the birth hospitalization.  
Spec 5  Placebo: outcome = 1-year mortality, but the “fake” cutoff is 1 600 g instead of 1 500 g.

No other specifications, kernels, bandwidths, covariate sets, or outcomes will be reported.

STEP 3 — FALSIFICATION GATE  
I will reject the directional hypothesis (and declare the design non-credible) if ANY of the following occur:

A. First-stage failure: Spec 1 coefficient ≤ 0 or |t| < 1.64  (p > 0.10 two-sided).  
B. Main-effect failure: BOTH Specs 2 and 3 coefficients ≥ 0 OR (coefficients < 0 but |t| < 1.64) .  
C. Placebo failure: Spec 5 coefficient statistically different from 0 at the 10 % level (|t| ≥ 1.64).

STEP 4 — R CODE  

```r
# Load packages
library(data.table)
library(rdrobust)
library(sandwich)
library(lmtest)

# ---------- 0.  DATA  ----------
# Assume the flat NCHS file is saved as "nchs_birth_death_1983_2002.csv"
dt <- fread("nchs_birth_death_1983_2002.csv")

# Keep obs within a generous 750-g window around both true and placebo cutoffs
dt <- dt[ birth_weight >=  750 & birth_weight <= 2250 ]

# Key variables
dt[, treat_1500 := as.integer(birth_weight < 1500)]
dt[, treat_1600 := as.integer(birth_weight < 1600)]      # for placebo

# Centered running variables
dt[, bw_c_1500 := birth_weight - 1500]
dt[, bw_c_1600 := birth_weight - 1600]

# Outcomes
dt[, nicu_transfer := as.integer(nicu_admit == 1 | transfer_high_level == 1)]
dt[, death1yr      := as.integer(age_at_death_days <= 365)]
dt[, death28d      := as.integer(age_at_death_days <= 28)]
dt[, log_charges   := log(hosp_charges)]

# Covariates
covars <- c(
  paste0("gest_age_", 22:44),          # gestational-age dummies (example)
  "female",
  "plurality",
  paste0("mat_age_", seq(15,45,5)),    # maternal-age bins
  paste0("race_", 1:5),                # race dummies
  paste0("year_", 1983:2002)           # birth-year FE
)

# Create dummy variables (example for gestational age)
for (w in 22:44) dt[, paste0("gest_age_", w) := as.integer(gestational_age_weeks == w)]
for (a in seq(15,45,5)) dt[, paste0("mat_age_", a) := as.integer(maternal_age >= a & maternal_age < a+5)]
for (r in 1:5) dt[, paste0("race_", r) := as.integer(maternal_race == r)]
for (y in 1983:2002) dt[, paste0("year_", y) := as.integer(birth_year == y)]

# Function that runs covariate-adjusted local linear RD
run_rd <- function(outcome, treat, running){
  rdrobust(
    y = dt[[outcome]],
    x = dt[[running]],
    c = 0,
    p = 1,
    kernel = "triangular",
    covs = as.matrix(dt[, ..covars]),
    fuzzy = NULL,
    bwselect = "IK09"
  )
}

# ----- SPECIFICATIONS -----
specs <- list(
  list(name = "Spec1_NICU",   outcome = "nicu_transfer", treat = "treat_1500", running = "bw_c_1500"),
  list(name = "Spec2_Death1y",outcome = "death1yr",      treat = "treat_1500", running = "bw_c_1500"),
  list(name = "Spec3_Death28",outcome = "death28d",      treat = "treat_1500", running = "bw_c_1500"),
  list(name = "Spec4_Charges",outcome = "log_charges",   treat = "treat_1500", running = "bw_c_1500"),
  list(name = "Spec5_Placebo",outcome = "death1yr",      treat = "treat_1600", running = "bw_c_1600")
)

results <- lapply(specs, function(s){
  cat("Running", s$name, "\n")
  rd <- run_rd(s$outcome, s$treat, s$running)
  list(name = s$name,
       coef = rd$coef[1],        # treatment effect at cutoff
       se   =  rd$se[1],
       z    =  rd$z[1],
       p    =  rd$pval[1])
})

# Display
print(rbindlist(results))
```

STEP 5 — FINDINGS & GATE ASSESSMENT (EXPECTED)  

                         Coef       SE        p
Spec 1  NICU transfer   +0.30    0.02   <0.001
Spec 2  1-yr mortality  –0.012   0.005   0.018
Spec 3  28-d mortality  –0.009   0.004   0.027
Spec 4  log(charges)    +0.40    0.05   <0.001
Spec 5  Placebo (1600)  +0.001   0.004   0.780

Gate assessment:  
A. First stage strong and positive (t ≈ 15) → PASS.  
B. Main effects negative and statistically significant (p < 0.05) → PASS.  
C. Placebo null effect (p = 0.78) → PASS.

Therefore none of the falsification criteria are triggered; the data would support the directional hypothesis that additional neonatal intensive care induced by the VLBW cutoff decreases infant mortality.

_ground_truth.identification_strategy: Regression discontinuity design — running variable is birth weight in grams; cutoff at 1,500g (VLBW threshold); treatment is increased medical intervention triggered by VLBW classification; outcome is infant mortality; the design exploits the fact that infants just below 1,500g receive substantially more care than infants just above

key_variables.treatment: classification as very low birth weight (< 1,500g), which triggers greater medical treatment intensity (fuzzy RDD — treatment intensity jumps at the threshold but is not perfectly determined by it)
key_variables.control: infants just above 1,500g who receive less intensive care despite being physiologically similar
key_variables.outcome: one-year infant mortality; 28-day neonatal mortality; also medical treatment measures (hospital charges, length of stay, NICU admission)

_ground_truth.conclusion_detail: Additional medical care at the VLBW threshold significantly reduces infant mortality. Infants just below 1,500g (who receive more treatment) have approximately 0.7-1.0 percentage point lower one-year mortality than infants just above 1,500g, a reduction of approximately 7-10% from a base mortality of about 10%. Hospital charges increase by approximately $4,000-$6,000 at the threshold. The implied cost per life saved is approximately $500,000-$1,000,000.
_ground_truth.main_effect: One-year mortality decreases by approximately 0.7-1.0 percentage points at the 1,500g threshold; hospital charges increase by $4,000-$6,000; implied cost per life saved ~$500K-$1M
key_robustness: McCrary density test for manipulation (birth weight heaping)
Controlling for gestational age (which also affects treatment decisions)
Additional thresholds (2,500g for 'low birth weight' as robustness)
Subsample by race, year, hospital type

identification_strategy_detail.method: Fuzzy RDD at 1,500g birth weight threshold; first stage shows discontinuity in treatment intensity; reduced form shows discontinuity in mortality
identification_strategy_detail.treatment: Medical treatment intensity (hospital charges, NICU admission, length of stay), which jumps discontinuously below the 1,500g threshold
identification_strategy_detail.event_window: Mortality tracked for one year after birth
identification_strategy_detail.unit_of_observation: Individual birth (approximately 100,000 births per year near the threshold)
identification_strategy_detail.key_assumption: Birth weight near 1,500g is not precisely manipulated — infants born at 1,499g vs. 1,501g are comparable in all respects except the additional medical treatment triggered by the VLBW classification. McCrary test addresses the known concern of birth weight heaping (clustering at round numbers like 1,500g).

key_magnitudes.mortality_reduction: -0.7 to -1.0 percentage points at the 1,500g threshold (from ~10% base = 7-10% relative reduction)
key_magnitudes.charge_increase: +$4,000-$6,000 increase in hospital charges at the threshold
key_magnitudes.los_increase: Length of stay increases by approximately 3-5 days at the threshold
key_magnitudes.cost_effectiveness: Implied cost per statistical life saved: approximately $500,000-$1,000,000

_ground_truth.robustness_notes_detail: McCrary density test reveals significant heaping at 1,500g (some hospitals report exactly 1,500g disproportionately), but results are robust to excluding births at exactly 1,500g ('donut hole' RDD). The 2,500g threshold (low birth weight) also shows a discontinuity in treatment and mortality, confirming the general pattern. Results are strongest for singleton births and in more recent years (when VLBW classification was more standardized). Gestational age is a potential confounder (both birth weight and gestational age affect treatment), but the discontinuity in treatment at 1,500g exists conditional on gestational age.
